claims.text: The synthesis is a polyol process conducted at 473 K.
The target nanoparticles comprise Pt, Pd, Au, and Ag alloyed with early transition metals such as Ti or V.
A strong reducing agent produces faster reduction than a mild reducing agent under the proposed conditions.
Fast reduction kinetically traps non-equilibrium short-range atomic ordering in the nanoparticles.
Slow reduction yields near-equilibrium random mixing in the nanoparticles.
Reducing-agent strength is the only intentionally varied synthesis parameter in the controlled comparison.
Rapid reduction causes a higher nucleation rate.
A high nucleation rate kinetically traps local clusters or ordered arrangements of metal atoms.
Slower reduction gives the system more opportunity to approach equilibrium and form a more uniform atomic distribution.
Differences in atomic ordering alter the distribution and density of catalytic active sites.
Differences in atomic ordering affect adsorption energies and catalytic reaction pathways.
Fast-reduced nanoparticles will exhibit catalytic activity different from that of the slow-reduced baseline in CO oxidation.
The catalytic-performance difference will coincide with a detectable difference in atomic ordering.
High-resolution TEM and XPS mapping can verify the proposed differences in atomic-scale ordering and elemental distribution.
The hypothesis is expected to apply near 473 K in controlled polyol synthesis for the specified noble-metal and early-transition-metal systems.
Significant changes in temperature, solvent, or metal composition may cause departures from the hypothesized behavior.
Particle-size distribution and defect density may confound the relationship between atomic ordering and catalytic performance.
